warn.EPOCH_LOW_COVERAGE: A short revisit is shown as a low coverage epoch. It is not used in measurements.
warn.MOVING_TARGET: Frames follow the moving target: each exposure is centered on the JPL Horizons position at its own mid time, so the stars move between frames and trail in the stacks.
warn.NO_APERTURE_CORRECTION: The brightness of the coma is an aperture sum without an aperture correction, so absolute values are lower limits of the total.
warn.NO_SPACECRAFT_POSITION: The spacecraft position was not available for some exposures, so their positions are geocentric, without the topocentric correction.
warn.IMAGES_FAILED: Some images could not be processed and are missing from the sequence.

barnard.name: Barnard's Star
barnard.headline: The fastest-moving star in our sky, seen moving by SPHEREx
barnard.look: A bright dot stepping north, about one pixel every six months, while every other star stays put.
barnard.limit: Core saturated in all six detectors. Centroids come from a PSF-wing fit in D5 and D6, core masked.
barnard.caption: The dot moving up is Barnard's Star. It crosses about one pixel between epochs, six months apart.

wise0855.name: WISE 0855-0714
wise0855.headline: The coldest known brown dwarf crossing the infrared sky
wise0855.look: A faint dot stepping west in D5 and D6. Switch to D1 and it disappears: it gives off almost no light below 3 µm.
wise0855.limit: Too faint to see below 3 µm. With three epochs, parallax is fixed to the published value.
wise0855.caption: The faint dot moving right is WISE 0855-0714, the coldest known brown dwarf. It only shows up at 4 to 5 µm.

epsindib.name: Epsilon Indi B
epsindib.headline: Two brown dwarfs travelling together, seen as one point
epsindib.look: One dot moving down and to the left, south-east. It is really two objects less than 1 arcsec apart.
epsindib.limit: SPHEREx pixels are 6.2 arcsec, so the pair cannot be split. Bright ε Indi A, 400 arcsec away, adds scattered light.
epsindib.caption: The dot moving down and left is Epsilon Indi B: two brown dwarfs too close together for SPHEREx to separate.

rwaur.name: RW Aurigae
rwaur.headline: A young star that flickers as dust passes in front of it
rwaur.look: The dot at the center stays put but fades and recovers. Neighbouring stars keep a steady brightness.
rwaur.measuredLabel: D3 flux change, E2 vs E1
rwaur.limit: Its companion 1.5 arcsec away is blended in. Quick Release fluxes are preliminary.
rwaur.caption: RW Aurigae stays in place but fades and recovers between epochs, as clouds of dust pass in front of it.

rdra.name: R Draconis
rdra.headline: A pulsating giant star that changes brightness over months
rdra.look: The bright star at the center swells and fades. Open Spectrum to see its water bands change too.
rdra.measuredLabel: Broadband flux change, E2 vs E1
rdra.limit: Bright enough to saturate D1 in some exposures. Spectral shape changes with pulsation phase.
rdra.caption: R Draconis is a giant star that pulses. Watch it dim and brighten between epochs, about six months apart.

sci.title: Seeing the sky move
sci.lead: In 1930 a young astronomer found Pluto by flipping between two photographs of the same stars. Destello does the same thing with NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey, for any patch of the sky.

s1.p1: At Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, Clyde Tombaugh was searching for a planet beyond Neptune. He photographed the same region of sky a few nights apart, then put the two glass plates in a blink comparator: a viewer that flips quickly between them.
s1.p2: Hundreds of thousands of stars stayed still. One faint dot jumped back and forth. It was Pluto. Destello applies the same idea to SPHEREx images taken months apart.

s2.p1: SPHEREx is a NASA space telescope that maps the entire sky in infrared light. It was built to study how the universe began, how galaxies grew, and where the water and ice in planet-forming clouds come from.
s2.p2: To do that it photographs every part of the sky again roughly every six months. Those repeat visits are what Destello uses: each visit is one epoch, and comparing epochs shows what moved or changed.

s3.p1: SPHEREx has six detectors, D1 to D6. Each sits behind a filter whose color changes smoothly across its surface, so a single image is not one color. Together the detectors cover 0.75 to 5.0 micrometers, all of it invisible to our eyes.
s3.p2: In Destello you can watch any one detector, or All of them combined. The band edges below are the nominal design values.
s3.caption: Nominal wavelength coverage of each detector. The exact band seen at a given pixel is read from the image headers.

s4.p1: During one visit SPHEREx photographs a patch many times over one to a few weeks, each time at a slightly different color. A single exposure is noisy, so Destello sorts the exposures by detector and combines each group into one coadd.
s4.p2: Before combining, it subtracts the glow of zodiacal dust, masks flagged pixels and aligns everything to one grid. One brightness scale is shared by all epochs of a detector, so a star that looks fainter really is fainter.

s5.p1: A difference image subtracts one epoch from another. First Destello scales the two so steady stars match in brightness, since each coadd samples a slightly different mix of colors. Then it subtracts, pixel by pixel.
s5.p2: Anything steady cancels to gray. A moving object leaves a pair: blue where it was, orange where it is now. An object that only changes brightness leaves one color and no pair.

s6.p1: SPHEREx was built to map the whole sky in many colors, not to take sharp pictures. These limits are shown in the Explorer too, next to the data they affect.

l1.d: A SPHEREx pixel is about 6.2 arcsec. Close pairs cannot be split and crowded fields blend.

l2.d: Motion needs at least two epochs, and the current release has only a few. Fits with three epochs are uncertain.

l3.d: Very bright stars saturate some detectors. Their centroids use the unsaturated wings or another detector.

l4.t: Faint objects need the right detector
l4.d: Cold brown dwarfs are almost invisible below 3 micrometers. Choose D5 or D6 for them.

l5.d: Quick Release fluxes are preliminary and may change in later releases.

l6.d: Catalog positions are propagated to each frame time with proper motion. A coordinate without a stated epoch can be off by many pixels.

s7.p1: Destello uses data from NASA SPHEREx served by NASA/IPAC IRSA, Gaia DR3 (ESA), CatWISE2020, SIMBAD and Sesame (CDS) and JPL Small-Body Identification. The full acknowledgements are on the About page.

val.title: Destello against published values
val.lead: Destello finds the same source in every SPHEREx epoch, centroids it and fits a linear motion. We compare the result with values from the literature and from Gaia. Every row below is read from the latest validation run, nothing is typed by hand.
val.unavailTitle: Validation results are not available yet
val.unavailBody: The server has not published a validation run. This page shows results only when they exist, so nothing is displayed in their place.
val.errorBody: The validation results could not be loaded. Try again in a moment.
val.caption: Tolerance is the largest accepted difference between Destello and the published value, in units of the combined 1 sigma uncertainty.
val.resAria: Residual position of {{name}} in right ascension and declination in each epoch, in arcsec.
val.resNote: Residuals are the distance of each epoch centroid from the fitted straight-line motion.
val.limitsTitle: Limits and how Destello handles them
val.limitsIntro: These limits come from the instrument and from the data releases. Each one states what Destello does about it and what was measured on the test targets of this report.

l1.b: SPHEREx returns to a position about every six months, so a field has only a few epochs and a fitted motion carries a large uncertainty.
l1.d: Every image of every public release is used, a sequence is rebuilt when IRSA publishes new data, and each fit reports its uncertainty and the number of epochs behind it.
l1.mMotion: Fitted proper motions differ from the published values by {{min}} to {{max}} percent.

l2.b: A pixel covers about 6.2 arcsec. Sources closer than that are not resolved, and no processing separates them.
l2.d: Centroids are measured to a fraction of a pixel and compared with catalog positions propagated to each epoch. A pair that cannot be resolved is stated as unresolved.
l2.mCentroid: Observed positions lie a median of {{median}} arcsec ({{fraction}} of a pixel) from the propagated catalog position, and at most {{max}} arcsec.

l3.b: The astrometry and photometry of a Quick Release are preliminary and may change in later releases.
l3.d: Each epoch is tied again to Gaia DR3 field stars before measuring, the flux scale is checked against 2MASS, and every result records the release it came from.
l3.mAstrometry: Median offset from Gaia DR3: {{before}} arcsec as delivered, {{after}} arcsec after recalibration.
l3.mFlux: Flux scale between {{min}} and {{max}} of 2MASS, on {{stars}} field stars per band.

l4.t: A test that cannot be run is not a pass
l4.b: A target that cannot be measured is reported as not measurable with the reason, never as a pass.

l5.b: Differences are computed against the combined uncertainty of Destello and the published value.

m1.b: Every SPHEREx image that covers the position is grouped into epochs by observation time and combined per detector.

m2.b: Each epoch is aligned to Gaia DR3 stars in the same field, after propagating them to the observation time.

m3.b: A point-spread-function fit gives a position and an uncertainty for every epoch. Flagged pixels are excluded.

m4.b: A straight line in position against time gives the proper motion. Parallax is fixed to the catalog value.

m5.b: The difference to the published value is divided by the combined uncertainty. A test passes when it is below its tolerance.

val.data: Data: SPHEREx spectral images via NASA IRSA. Astrometric reference: Gaia DR3 (ESA/Gaia/DPAC), read through the NASA MAST copy.
val.failNote: Failing tests are shown as they are, with the measured values and the reason for each result.
val.resTwo: Targets with fewer than three epochs have no residual plot: a straight line fits two points exactly.

r.fluxReference: The IRSA Spectrophotometry Tool offers no programmatic access, so 2MASS is the independent reference.

Epsilon Indi B: {{index}} ± {{err}}. {{n}} field stars: median {{median}}, robust scatter {{scatter}}. Depth below the field: {{depth}} sigma. Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb are unresolved, so this is their combined light.

r.methane_not_measurable_target: Not measurable: no epoch of the target has all three wavelength windows measured.

r.window_below_snr: Not measurable: the CO2 band window (4.23 to 4.27 µm) and its two continuum windows each hold the 2 points required (band {{nBand}}, blue {{nBlue}}, red {{nRed}}), but at least one window mean is detected below 3 sigma (S/N: band {{snrBand}}, blue {{snrBlue}}, red {{snrRed}}). No detection is claimed.
r.band_excess_continuum_undetected: CO2 band flux {{bandFlux}} ± {{bandErr}} Jy against a continuum of {{cont}} ± {{contErr}} Jy, which is not detected (S/N: blue {{snrBlue}}, red {{snrRed}}) and is interpolated linearly in flux. Band minus continuum: {{sig}} sigma; {{sigUpper}} sigma above the continuum 3 sigma upper limit of {{upper}} Jy. No ratio is reported for an undetected continuum. Usable points in the blue, band and red windows: {{blue}}, {{band}}, {{red}}.
r.band_excess: CO2 band flux {{bandFlux}} Jy against a continuum of {{cont}} Jy: excess {{excess}} ± {{err}} (band over continuum, minus 1), {{sig}} sigma. Usable points in the blue, band and red windows: {{blue}}, {{band}}, {{red}}.
r.ephemeris_check: {{within}} of {{measured}} measured exposures lie within their position bound of the JPL Horizons position ({{total}} exposures in the campaign). Median offset {{median}} arcsec, largest {{max}} arcsec.
r.ephemeris_check_neighbours: {{current}} The centroid fits the Gaia DR3 stars in the fit box together with the comet (method changed on 2026-11-15, after the earlier result was known). With a single Gaussian, the earlier method: {{within}} of {{measured}} measured exposures within the bound.
r.recalibration_catalog_not_gaia: Not measurable by rule: the recalibration catalog is not Gaia DR3, which the long-baseline fit requires.
r.no_wise_companion: Not measurable: no WISE companion sequence has been built for this target.
r.too_few_epochs_per_mission: Not measurable: {{wise}} WISE and NEOWISE epochs and {{spherex}} SPHEREx epochs were measured, and at least 2 are required from each mission.
r.long_baseline_fit: Combined fit of {{total}} epochs ({{wise}} WISE and NEOWISE, {{spherex}} SPHEREx): proper motion {{pmra}} ± {{pmraErr}} mas/yr in right ascension (times cos declination) and {{pmdec}} ± {{pmdecErr}} mas/yr in declination, at epoch J{{epoch}}.

pages2.aboutP1: Destello is a free, bilingual web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx all-sky infrared images into time-lapses of any patch of sky. Type a name or a position and it finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, combines them by epoch and plays them in turn.
pages2.aboutP2: It is made for students, teachers and citizen scientists first, with enough provenance for astronomers to trust what they see. Destello is Spanish for a flash or a glint: the moment a moving star catches your eye.
pages2.challengeBody: Destello was built in 48 hours for the challenge Planet X and SPHEREx. The challenge asked for a way to blink SPHEREx images, query any position by URL, overlay Gaia and WISE catalogs, and make the result embeddable.
pages2.teamBody: Destello is built by team Never be Frog. The sole member is Felipe Cabrera Bisio, from Montevideo, Uruguay. It was made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge Planet X and SPHEREx.
pages2.licenceBody: The source code is released under the MIT licence.
pages2.nonEndorse: Destello is an independent project built by team Never be Frog (Felipe Cabrera Bisio) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not an official product of NASA, Caltech/IPAC or JPL, and their names do not imply endorsement.
pages2.scienceIntro: How the images are made and what they can and cannot show is explained on the Science page.

share2.ctlNoteFull: Playback, speed, loop and epoch timeline.

SATURATION.b: Saturated or flagged pixels fall inside the measurement aperture. Those exposures carry no flux value, and a centroid relies on the faint outer part of the star.

PSF_WINGS_CENTROID.b: The star is saturated at its center in every epoch. Each position comes from fits to the unflagged outer part of the star on single exposures, averaged per epoch.

BLENDED_SOURCE.b: Another source lies within about one SPHEREx pixel of the target. Positions and motion are less certain than their error bars suggest.

EPSILON_INDI_UNRESOLVED.b: Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb are separated by less than 1 arcsec and SPHEREx pixels are about 6.2 arcsec, so the pair is unresolved and the measurement refers to both together.

NO_REDUNDANCY.b: Two epochs determine the motion exactly. There is no chi-square, and the uncertainty rests on the per-epoch errors alone.

PARALLAX_UNKNOWN.b: No parallax is known for this position, so it is fixed to zero.

QUICK_RELEASE_CALIBRATION.b: SPHEREx Quick Release calibration is preliminary and can carry systematic errors.

RECALIBRATION_UNAVAILABLE.b: Fewer than three reference stars were available in at least one epoch, so the archive coordinates were used there without a local correction.

NO_APERTURE_CORRECTION.b: Fluxes are sums inside the aperture and miss the faint wings of the star, so they are lower limits of the total flux.

PRESET_ASTROMETRY_USED.b: The position was moved to the time of each exposure with the catalog proper motion of this target.

POSITION_NOT_PROPAGATED.b: No proper motion was given, so the same position is used for every exposure.

OVERFLOW_PIXELS_USED.b: Some unflagged points include core pixels that reached the onboard overflow threshold, about half of full well. Their values come from the samples taken before the threshold and are kept, following the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement.

PARALLAX_FIXED.b: Fitting the parallax needs four or more epochs over at least one year, so it was fixed to the reference value.

TOO_FEW_EPOCHS.b: The source was measured in fewer than two epochs in this detector, so no motion can be fitted.

spec2.satNoneBody: Every exposure has saturated or flagged pixels in the aperture, so Destello withholds the flux instead of showing a wrong number. This is a measurement limit, not an error.

player.title: The blink player
player.body: The same patch of sky, imaged by SPHEREx on each survey pass, about six months apart. Each square is one image pixel at its real resolution, never smoothed. Steady stars stay in place; an object that moves jumps between frames.

search.title: Choose a sky position
search.body: Type coordinates (RA and Dec) or an object name in the search box, or open one of the presets. Each preset is a known object chosen to show motion or variability.

transport.title: Play and step through the epochs
transport.body: Play the sequence, or step through it one epoch at a time. The timeline lists every epoch with its date; select one to go straight to it. All epochs of a detector share one brightness scale, so a change between frames is in the data, not in the display.

detector.title: Choose a detector
detector.body: SPHEREx observes with six detectors, each covering its own range of infrared wavelengths. Switch detectors to compare how the field looks at different wavelengths.

mode.title: Difference mode
mode.body: Difference mode subtracts a reference epoch from the epoch on screen. Steady sources cancel out, and a source that moved leaves a pair of opposite residuals.

overlays.title: Catalog overlays
overlays.body: Turn on Gaia and CatWISE to mark known sources where each catalog places them on the date of the epoch on screen. A moving source without a marker deserves a closer look.

results.title: Results, measurements and spectrum
results.body: For a preset, the result card compares the motion measured in SPHEREx with the published value. The Measure tab measures the selected source in each epoch, and the Spectrum tab shows its spectrum and light curve.

motion.title: Motion search
motion.body: Motion search looks for sources that move consistently across all epochs of the sequence. It runs only on request. Each entry is a candidate to review, to be checked against catalogs and the images before any conclusion.

share.title: Share and export
share.body: Share copies a link that reopens this exact view, or a code to embed it in another page. Export saves the sequence as an animated GIF with its data credits. The tour can be replayed from Guided tour at the top of the page.

report.title: Report a candidate
report.markIntro: Click the source in the player, in at least two epochs. Step with ← and →. Each mark is saved for the epoch on screen.
report.keyboardHelp: Place a mark in the epoch on screen, then move it one pixel at a time. North is up, east is left.

report.checking: Searching four catalogs around each mark. Positions are propagated to each mark's date, so known movers are caught too.
report.geocentric: SBIdent assumes a geocentric observer while SPHEREx is in low Earth orbit, so very near objects are matched only approximately. Its positions are computed at the mid time of each epoch coadd, which spans about two weeks.

proxima.name: Proxima Centauri
proxima.why: The closest known star to the Sun, about 4.2 light years away. It crosses about 3.9 arcsec of sky per year.

teegarden.name: Teegarden's Star
teegarden.why: A faint red dwarf about 12.5 light years away, only identified in 2003 by searching archival survey data for fast movers. It moves about 5.1 arcsec per year.

vanmaanen.name: Van Maanen 2
vanmaanen.why: The closest known solitary white dwarf, about 14 light years away, discovered in 1917 through its motion of about 3 arcsec per year.

wolf359.name: Wolf 359
wolf359.why: One of the nearest stars, a red dwarf about 7.9 light years away moving about 4.7 arcsec per year.

kapteyn.name: Kapteyn's Star
kapteyn.why: An old halo subdwarf about 12.8 light years away. Its motion of about 8.6 arcsec per year is the second largest known, after Barnard's Star.

groombridge1830.name: Groombridge 1830
groombridge1830.why: A metal-poor star from the Galactic halo crossing the solar neighbourhood at high speed, about 7 arcsec per year.

lacaille9352.name: Lacaille 9352
lacaille9352.why: A red dwarf about 10.7 light years away moving about 6.9 arcsec per year.

trappist1.name: TRAPPIST-1
trappist1.why: An ultracool dwarf about 41 light years away with seven known Earth-sized planets. It moves about 1 arcsec per year, less than one SPHEREx pixel per decade.

ross128.name: Ross 128
ross128.why: A quiet red dwarf about 11 light years away that hosts a temperate planet. It moves about 1.4 arcsec per year.

v1647ori.name: V1647 Orionis
v1647ori.why: A young star whose accretion outbursts lit up McNeil's Nebula in 2004 and again in 2008. Its infrared brightness changes over months.

fuori.name: FU Orionis
fuori.why: The prototype of FU Orionis outbursts: it brightened by about six magnitudes in 1937 and is still fading slowly.

ttau.name: T Tauri
ttau.why: The prototype of young, still contracting T Tauri stars, with irregular brightness changes.

boyajian.name: Boyajian's Star
boyajian.why: A star whose irregular dimming, up to about 22 percent, was found in Kepler data and is still debated.

sn2023ixf.name: SN 2023ixf
sn2023ixf.why: A Type II supernova in the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), discovered in May 2023 and one of the nearest of the decade. By the SPHEREx epochs it may have faded below detection.

motion.agreement: differs from the catalog by {{value}} sigma
motion.noDistance: Parallax not significant: no distance given
motion.matchParallax: catalog parallax {{value}} mas, differs by {{sigma}} sigma
motion.parallaxFitted: The epochs span at least a year, so the parallax is fitted with the motion; a distance is given only when the parallax reaches {{sigma}} sigma.
motion.parallaxFixed: With these epochs the parallax cannot be separated from the motion, so it is not fitted.

limits.title: Limits of this search
limits.linear: Only motion in a straight line at constant speed across the searched epochs is found.
limits.saturated: Saturated and flagged pixels are excluded, so very bright sources can be missed or measured with larger errors.
limits.parallax: Parallax is fitted only when four or more epochs span at least a year. With fewer epochs it is not modeled, and a nearby source, which also shifts between survey passes because of the orbit of the Earth, gets larger errors.
limits.lowCoverage: Low coverage epochs (short revisits) are not searched.
limits.distant: A distant solar system object, such as a hypothetical Planet X, shifts by arcminutes between survey passes, mostly from the parallax of the orbit of the Earth, far outside the linear motions searched here; it cannot be found this way.

err.TOO_FEW_EPOCHS: The motion search needs three or more full coverage epochs. This view has fewer.
err.NO_FITS: No detector coadd of this view could be measured, so no search was made.
err.RATE_LIMITED: Too many searches in a short time. Wait a moment and try again.
err.NOT_FOUND: This view is no longer available on the server. Reload the page to build it again.
err.DEMO_UNAVAILABLE: The motion search is not cached in the demo for this view.
err.network: The server did not answer. Check the connection and try again.
err.generic: The motion search failed. Try again.

home.title: Destello: watch the infrared sky move with NASA SPHEREx
home.description: Blink real NASA SPHEREx infrared images of any sky position across survey epochs, so that moving and variable objects such as stars and comets stand out.

science.description: How Destello turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into epoch coadds, blink time-lapses and difference images, and what the images can and cannot show.

validation.description: Destello compared with published values: proper motions, variability and astrometry measured in SPHEREx images, with every pass, failure and unmeasurable test.

about.title: About
about.description: Destello is a free, bilingual tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge Planet X and SPHEREx. What it does, who it is for and its data credits.

hunt.description: Review real SPHEREx images of one sky field at a time and mark what changes between epochs, as a volunteer search for moving objects in the infrared sky.

story.description: A short tour of how astronomers find moving objects, from the 1930 discovery of Pluto with two photographic plates to the infrared sky of NASA SPHEREx.

comet.description: Follow the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in NASA SPHEREx images across survey epochs, with its motion and infrared spectrum measured from the data.

learn.description: A classroom activity: find Barnard's Star in real SPHEREx images, mark it in each epoch, calculate its proper motion and compare it with the Gaia catalog value.

guide.description: A printable 40 minute lesson plan for teachers: students measure the proper motion of Barnard's Star in SPHEREx images and compare it with a catalog value.

developers.description: Use Destello from code: the public API, the embeddable player, the URL contract, the rate limits and the data resources behind every frame of the time-lapse.

embed.title: Embedded player
embed.description: Embeddable Destello player that blinks the NASA SPHEREx epochs of one sky position. It is meant for other websites and is not indexed by search engines.

report.description: A candidate moving source marked by a visitor in several SPHEREx epochs, with automated checks against catalogs. The candidate is unconfirmed.

target.description: Blink real NASA SPHEREx infrared images of {{name}} across survey epochs and see how it moves or changes against the fixed background stars.

error.description: This page could not be shown. Return to the Destello home page to explore NASA SPHEREx images of any sky position.
